zone: Stehekin and the Agnes Creek country
_areas_note: ALL SIX PEAKS HELD, and unusually for these batches the grouping was right — every one of them is a boat-and-shuttle objective and none is reachable by driving. They sit in what climbers call the Stehekin triangle, the block of big peaks bounded by Lake Chelan on the east, the Stehekin River on the north, Agnes Creek on the west and Railroad Creek on the south, and the only ways into it are the passenger boat up the lake or a multi-day walk over a pass from somewhere else. THE BOAT IS THE TRIP AND EVERYTHING BELOW IS SUBORDINATE TO IT — see the landing entry, which is written first for that reason rather than because anyone climbs from it. Agnes Mountain, Needle Peak, Dark Peak and Mount Lyall all hang off the Agnes Creek trail south from High Bridge; McGregor Mountain climbs straight out of the valley road a mile from the same bus stop; Flora Mountain is the outlier, reached from the Company Creek road on the lower valley rather than from High Bridge at all, and it is kept because it is the same boat, the same shuttle and the same permit system. WHAT IS NOT REPEATED: Cottonwood Camp and Basin Creek at the head of the Stehekin road are covered in the Cascade Pass file, the Bridge Creek trail camps north of the valley are covered in the Mount Goode file, and Bird Creek Camp on the Devore Creek trail — which is one of the two normal bases for Flora Mountain — is covered in the Sawtooth Ridge and Lake Chelan shore file alongside Devore and Tupshin. Flora therefore gets its Company Creek and Hilgard Pass side here, which nothing else has described, rather than a second write-up of Bird Creek. Hemlock Camp on the upper Agnes is deliberately not offered: insect-killed trees have been falling into it and it should not be used. TWO CURRENT FACTS worth checking before committing. The valley shuttle for the 2026 season is being run by a private operator rather than the park's own bus, with a different timetable and charter pricing outside it. And Holden Village, which is the back door into this country from the south by way of Railroad Creek, is closed to hikers for the 2026 summer and cannot supply, feed or house anybody — so a traverse that planned to resupply there does not work this year.

sites.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
sites.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.
sites.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
sites.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
sites.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.

sites.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
sites.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.
sites.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
sites.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
sites.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.

sites.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
sites.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.
sites.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
sites.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
sites.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.

sites.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
sites.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.
sites.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
sites.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
sites.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.

sites.name: West Fork Agnes Creek — the bivy under Agnes Mountain
sites.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.
sites.water: The West Fork itself for as long as you are beside it, which is most of the way. Above it, snowmelt only and only early in the season. There is no reason to be short of water low down and every reason to carry it once you leave the creek.
sites.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required for any overnight, and off-trail nights are handled as cross-country camping rather than as a named site — say what ground you intend to use when you arrange it rather than booking a camp that does not exist. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
sites.notes: This is the working bivy zone for AGNES MOUNTAIN and it needs to be described honestly: THE TRAIL HAS ALL BUT VANISHED. What is marked on maps as the West Fork Agnes Creek trail is now a rough bushwhack up the drainage, last given any real maintenance a decade or more ago, and it leads nowhere except to the base of the mountain. Round trip from High Bridge is around seventeen miles of walking on top of the boat and the shuttle. The recommended line on the peak itself takes the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak first and then traverses to Agnes's south ridge, with short technical sections up to about 5.6 — so this is a climb rather than a scramble, on a peak that is seldom done precisely because the approach is so poor relative to its modest height. Navigation skill is not optional. Season is roughly July into September; earlier the creek is high and the brush is worse, later the days are too short for the mileage. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved ground and finding its own way up a drainage with no tread, this is the wrong objective.

sites.name: Company Creek and Hilgard Pass — the lower-valley approach to Flora Mountain
sites.capacity: Dispersed. There is workable ground in the upper Hilgard Creek basin and around the pass, room for a party or two, with nothing developed and no facilities. The lower valley has scattered spots along the trail.
sites.water: Company Creek and then Hilgard Creek for most of the climb, which is generous by the standards of these approaches. The pass itself and the ground above it are dry once the snow has gone, so fill in the basin before going up for the summit.
sites.permit: The trail leaves the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area about two miles up and enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, so the rules change under your feet. A North Cascades backcountry permit covers the recreation area portion and any park camps; the wilderness above is national forest ground with a free self-issued permit and no quota. Work out which side of the line you intend to sleep on before booking anything. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass considerations apply on the forest side. Store food properly throughout; fires are inappropriate at the pass and restrictions are usual lower down by midsummer.
sites.notes: FLORA MOUNTAIN is the peak in this zone that does not start at High Bridge, and sending a party up the valley for it wastes a day. The Company Creek road leaves the Stehekin road about five and a half miles from the landing — the shuttle will drop you — and the trail from it climbs steeply, fords Company Creek at around five miles, and then follows Hilgard Creek to Hilgard Pass at 6,700 ft. THE FORD IS THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: it is a real crossing and in a high-water year it is the reason parties turn back, so check the level with a ranger before you commit to the day. Flora is one of the hundred highest summits in the state at a little over 8,300 ft and its southwest side is a talus and boulder hop rather than a climb, so once you are in position the summit is not the work. It can also be taken from a camp in the Bird Creek drainage on the Devore Creek side, which is the more commonly described base and is covered elsewhere; the Company Creek line is the one that starts from the lower valley road and it suits a party already camped at Harlequin. The views on the way up over Tupshin and Devore are the best part of the walk. July into early October, and the larch colour late in that window is worth planning around.
